This method covers the determination of the dielectric breakdown voltage of insulating oils of petroleum origin. The method is applicable to liquid petroleum oils commonly used in cables, transformers, oil circuit breakers, and similar apparatus 
as an insulating and cooling medium. The suitability of this method for testing oils having viscosities of more than 19 
CSt ( mm2 
/ s ) (100 SUS ) at 40oC ( 104 oF ) has not been 
determined.

This method is more sensitive to the deleterious effects of moisture in solution 
than method D 877, especially when cellulose fibers are present in the oil.(D 877 is ASTM standard test method is recommended for acceptance of insulating 
liquid received from vendors in tank cars, tank trucks, drums, and liquid from 
power system apparatus rated below 230kv, using Disk Electrodes).

This method is recommended for testing filtered, degassed, dehydrated oil 
prior to and during the filling of power systems apparatus rated above 230 kv, 
and for testing samples of oil from the apparatus after filling.
It is also 
finding increased usage for testing oils from transformers in service.

This method is not recommended for, and should not be used for, acceptance tests 
on oil received from vendors in tank cars, tank trucks or drums.

The dielectric breakdown voltage of an insulating liquid is of importance as a measure of the liquids ability to withstand electric stress without failure. It serves to indicate the presence of contaminating agents such as water dirt, moist 
cellulose fibers, or conducting particles in the liquid, one or more of which may be present in significant concentrations when low breakdown voltages are obtained. However, 
a high dielectric breakdown voltage does not necessarily indicate the absence of 
all contaminants; it may merely indicate that the concentrations of contaminants 
that are present in the liquid between the electrodes are not large enough to 
affect deleteriously the average breakdown voltage of the liquid when tested by 
this method.

The oil (all cases of oils for transformers, for 
oil filled cables, for circuit breakers ) whether new or used contained in a 
specified apparatus, is subjected to an electric field with a continuously 
increasing rate of voltage rise, till the oil breakdown. This intended to reveal 
the extent of physical pollution by water and other suspended matter and the 
advisability of carrying out drying and filtration treatment before the oils are 
introduced into the apparatus for which they are intended.

The dielectric 
breakdown voltage is the voltage reached during the test at the time the first 
spark occurs between electrodes. Whether it be transient or established.

The 
dielectric breakdown voltage of a liquid at commercial power frequencies is 
affected by the degree of uniformity of the electric field, the area of the 
electrodes or volume of the liquid under maximum stress, the temperature of the 
liquid (especially as it affects the relative saturation level of moisture in 
solution), gassing tendencies of the liquid under the influence of electric 
stress, concentration of dissolved gases (especially if saturation levels are 
exceeded as result of sudden cooling or decrease in pressure, which may cause 
the formation of gas bubbles), incompatibility with materials of construction, 
and velocity of flow. A decrease in dielectric 
strength of the liquid can have an accentuated effect on the electric creepage 
strength of solid insulating materials immersed in the liquid.

If the breakdown voltage 
is not in the proper range for the conditioned oil due to the existence of 
moisture or impurities it is recommended to send another sample to central 
chemical laboratory to observe the result or carry out the test in the filed.
